_slice: The county tier — California realignment and the Harris County district layer
_note: Counties had been present in this corpus only as the place a city sits. This pass treats the county as a government tier in its own right, on both sides of the American comparison, and the two sides turn out to solve the same problem in opposite directions. California pushed health, welfare and public safety down to counties in two realignments, 1991 and 2011, and funds them with dedicated shares of the state sales tax and vehicle licence fees — so a Californian county is largely financed by Sacramento against formulas Sacramento writes. Texas gives counties almost no ordinance power at all and instead lets services be constituted as separate districts that levy their own property tax: flood control, hospital, emergency services, community college, port. Harris County's Assessor-Collector collects for seventy separate taxing entities. The sharpest finding is a negative one. California indexes an extraordinary amount — five different price indexes at last count — but indexes almost none of what it sends to counties. The 1991 Realignment base is a ratchet against 1991-92 percentages; its growth account references a September 1991 report; the county share of in-home supportive services escalates at a flat 4 percent named in statute; and the Proposition 172 within-county split is measured against 1993-94 property tax losses. Only the county-level Proposition 172 ratio reads anything current. A state that legislates against indexes for wages, rents, taxes and welfare grants declines to do so for the money it sends its own counties.

reports.title: Counties Annual Report (County Financial Transactions Report)
reports.description: The annual compilation of revenue, expenditure, fund balance, debt and staffing reported by all 58 California counties under Government Code §§12463 and 53891 — the county companion to the Cities Annual Report. Since 2014 it has been published as open data rather than a bound volume, which is a quiet but real change in what "published" means.

entries.covers: FY 2025-26 County Financial Transactions Report

release_schedule.rule: The Controller shall compile and publish reports of the financial transactions of each county, city, and special district pursuant to subdivision (a) on or before November 1 of each year following the end of the annual reporting period. (California Government Code § 12463(b))
release_schedule.note: The county's underlying fiscal-year-end (June 30) financial data must be submitted to the Controller within seven months of fiscal year close (per SCO's County FTR Instructions), and the Controller must then compile and publish the statewide compiled report on or before November 1 of the following calendar year, per Gov. Code §12463(b). The most recent statutory deadline (Nov 1, 2025, covering FY2024-25) has already passed relative to today (2026-08-11), so the next occurrence is Nov 1, 2026, covering FY2025-26. The compiled data is published on the open-data platform bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov rather than as a single static document/PDF, but the statutory publication deadline governs its timing.

reports.title: Health and Welfare Realignment Allocation (1991 Realignment)
reports.description: The monthly apportionment of the Local Revenue Fund to counties for mental health, social services and public health, funded by a half-cent of state sales tax and a share of vehicle license fees under Welfare and Institutions Code §§17600-17606.20. The 1991 settlement that moved a large block of health and welfare responsibility from the state to the counties, and the money with it.

entries.covers: September 2026 monthly realignment allocation/deposit

release_schedule.rule: Welfare and Institutions Code Section 17600.15(b): "For the 1992-93 fiscal year and fiscal years thereafter, of the sales tax proceeds from revenues deposited to the credit of the Local Revenue Fund, the Controller shall make monthly deposits to the Mental Health Subaccount, the Social Services Subaccount, and the Health Subaccount..." No specific day-of-month is specified in statute; since FY2013-14 the statute delegates scheduling authority to the Department of Finance (deposits made "pursuant to a schedule provided by the Department of Finance").
release_schedule.note: The SCO's Health and Welfare Realignment Allocation page (https://www.sco.ca.gov/ard_payments_realign.html) organizes materials by fiscal year (currently FY2025-2026) with subpages for Base, Reconciliation, AB 85 Breakdown, CalWORKs MOE, Mental Health, Public Health, and Social Services allocations, plus an Annual Letter/Instructions/Reports for county reporting. No page publishes a dated release calendar; the underlying cadence is governed by statute (monthly Controller deposits per WIC 17600.15(b)), consistent with the corpus's existing releases_per_year=12. Exact day-of-month deposit dates are set administratively by the Department of Finance and were not found published as a public calendar.

reports.title: Local Revenue Fund 2011 allocations and reconciliation (2011 Realignment)
reports.description: County allocation and annual reconciliation for the second, larger realignment: trial court security, community corrections, district attorney and public defender, juvenile justice, protective services and behavioural health, funded from a dedicated 1.0625 percent share of the state sales tax plus vehicle license fees and constitutionally protected by Proposition 30. Established by Government Code §30025.

entries.covers: FY 2025-26 Local Revenue Fund 2011 reconciliation report

release_schedule.rule: Government Code §30025: counties/cities-and-counties must document any Local Revenue Fund 2011 subaccount reallocations from the previous fiscal year by September 30, and 'The Controller shall make an annual report to the fiscal committees of the Legislature of transfers made.' California's official statutory-reports tracking system (agencyreports.ca.gov, entry for this report) records this Controller reconciliation report as required 'Annually' with a recurring due date of December 31, and lists explicit due dates for FY reconciliations from 12/31/2013 through 12/31/2036, most recently 12/31/2025 (already passed as of 2026-08-11).
release_schedule.note: The SCO's own report archive page (sco.ca.gov/ard_payments_lrf_recon.html) is a static list of past fiscal-year reconciliation reports with no posted calendar or explicit dates; the December 31 annual due date comes from California's official state reporting-requirements tracking database (agencyreports.ca.gov), which cites Gov. Code §30025 as authority and lists a consistent December 31 recurring due date through 2036. The statute itself specifies a September 30 county documentation deadline but does not spell out the exact December 31 day for the Controller's report in the text I could access.

reports.title: Half-Percent Sales Tax for Public Safety (Proposition 172)
reports.description: The apportionment of the Local Public Safety Fund created by Proposition 172 in 1993 — a permanent half-cent sales tax dedicated to public safety, allocated to each qualified county in proportion to its share of statewide taxable sales, with county auditors redistributing a portion to cities.

entries.covers: May 2026 Half-Cent Public Safety Sales Tax remittance advice (hcps_0526ra.xlsx)
June 2026 Half-Cent Public Safety Sales Tax remittance advice (hcps_0626ra.xlsx)
July 2026 Half-Cent Public Safety Sales Tax remittance advice (hcps_0726ra.xlsx), the most recent file posted as of 2026-08-11
Projected next monthly remittance advice (August 2026), following the observed monthly cadence

release_schedule.note: The SCO's fiscal-year page for the Half-Percent Sales Tax for Public Safety (Prop 172) lists individual monthly 'Remittance Advice' allocation spreadsheets named hcps_MMYYra.xlsx, one per month, plus a running 'Year to Date' file (hcps_2526fy.xlsx). As of 2026-08-11, files exist sequentially for Sept 2025 through July 2026 (11 consecutive months), consistent with a monthly (12/year) release cadence, matching the corpus's releases_per_year=12. No page states an exact day-of-month rule for posting, and no forward-looking calendar of exact dates was found — only the file-naming/posting pattern itself, so this is classified as observed-pattern rather than published-calendar. August 2026's file was not yet posted at time of research.

reports.title: Certification of Vehicle License Fee Adjustment Amount
reports.description: The annual certification in which each county auditor reports to the Controller the vehicle license fee adjustment amount for the county and every city in it — the property tax paid in lieu of vehicle license fee created by the 2004 swap. A transfer that stopped being about vehicles and became a function of assessed value.

entries.covers: FY 2026-27 Vehicle License Fee Adjustment Amount certification/compiled data

release_schedule.rule: California Revenue and Taxation Code Section 97.70(c)(5): "The Controller shall make the information available to the public in a readily accessible compiled electronic file via the Controller's internet website on or before September 1 of each year." (This follows each county auditor's report of the vehicle license fee adjustment amount to the Controller, due on or before June 30 of each fiscal year.)
release_schedule.note: The SCO page (ard_payments_vlfaa.html) hosts the certification form, notification letters, and fiscal-year historical records, but does not itself display a release calendar; the governing publication deadline comes from R&T Code 97.70(c)(5). Counties must report VLFAA data to the Controller by June 30 each year (per the FY2023-24 VLFAA notification letter and the statute), and the Controller must publish the compiled statewide file by September 1. The computed next date, 2026-09-01, is in the future relative to 2026-08-11.

reports.title: Taxable Sales in California
reports.publisher: California Department of Tax and Fee Administration
reports.description: Quarterly and annual statistics of retail activity as measured by transactions subject to sales and use tax, reported statewide by business type and broken down to counties and cities. The county-level series the public safety allocation ratio is computed from.

entries.covers: Q1 2026 (Jan-Mar 2026) Taxable Sales in California tables, preliminary
Q2 2026 (Apr-Jun 2026) Taxable Sales in California tables, projected preliminary release

release_schedule.note: CDTFA's own page describes this as 'a quarterly report on retail sales activity in California.' No published release calendar or stated day-count rule was found on the publisher's site (Open Data Portal Help/FAQ has no scheduling section). Live inspection of the Open Data Portal on 2026-08-11 showed all 7 'Current Taxable Sales Tables' datasets (statewide by business type, by county, by city, etc.) last updated 2026/08/07, with the newest quarter present being '2026 Q1 - preliminary' (Jan-Mar 2026, quarter-end 03/31/2026). That is a ~4-month lag between quarter-end and data release. The 4 'Historical Taxable Sales Tables' (finalized prior data) were last updated 2026/08/06, one day earlier, suggesting preliminary and finalized/historical tables are refreshed together each quarter. Only one full release cycle could be directly observed (site tooling did not allow retrieving prior quarters' exact release dates, and Wayback Machine has no captured snapshots of this dynamically-rendered page since 2022), so the projected Q2 2026 entry assumes the same ~4-month lag continues; it should be treated as an estimate rather than a confirmed date. releases_per_year=4 in the corpus is consistent with the publisher's own 'quarterly report' description.

reports.title: Constitutional Basis of County Government
reports.publisher: County Judges and Commissioners Association of Texas
reports.description: A structural context document, filed as a Texas House committee handout, setting out that Texas counties hold only powers the Legislature expressly grants and have severely limited ordinance authority — unlike home rule cities, which may adopt any ordinance not in conflict with state law. This is the reason the Texas county tier is so crowded with separate districts: services a California county would simply provide have to be pushed into bodies that levy their own tax.

reports.title: Harris County Truth-in-Taxation summary and tax rate calculation worksheets
reports.description: The Assessor-Collector's statutory disclosure library: adopted, maintenance-and-operations, debt, no-new-revenue and voter-approval rates for every taxing jurisdiction in the county under Tax Code §26.16, plus the underlying calculation worksheet for each jurisdiction each year. The office maintains around 1.5 million tax accounts and collects for 70 separate taxing entities — the single most useful document in the Texas county layer, because every district's rate is signed for in one place.

release_schedule.rule: Rate adopted by the later of September 30 or 60 days after the taxing unit receives the certified appraisal roll (Tex. Tax Code §26.05(a)).

entries.covers: 2026 tax rate adoption

release_schedule.note: Candidate edge, not yet added: this report depends on hcad-appraisal-roll's certification date by statute (§26.05(a) ties the rate-adoption deadline to when the certified roll is received) — needs a proper basis before becoming a real edge.

reports.title: Harris County Flood Control District Annual Comprehensive Financial Report
reports.description: Audited annual statements for the Flood Control District, created by the Legislature in 1937, governed by Commissioners Court and funded by its own dedicated ad valorem tax — $0.04966 per $100 for 2025. A separate levy for flood control is the kind of thing that exists nowhere in the Canadian or Californian material in this corpus.

entries.covers: ACFR for fiscal year ended 9/30/2023 (auditor's report dated 3/28/2024)
ACFR for fiscal year ended 9/30/2024 (auditor's report dated 4/8/2025)
ACFR for fiscal year ended 9/30/2025 (auditor's report dated 4/7/2026) - already published, current edition on site as of 2026-08-11
Projected next ACFR, for fiscal year ended 9/30/2026

release_schedule.note: No published release calendar or stated statutory deadline was found on the Harris County Auditor's site (auditor.harriscountytx.gov/Reports/Annual-Comprehensive-Financial-Report-Harris-County or /Pages/CAFR.aspx). However, the independent auditor's report date printed inside each year's PDF shows a very consistent pattern: FYE 9/30/2023 report dated 3/28/2024; FYE 9/30/2024 report dated 4/8/2025; FYE 9/30/2025 report dated 4/7/2026 (verified by downloading and text-extracting the actual PDFs from auditor.harriscountytx.gov/Portals/auditor/documents/ACFRs/). This is ~6 months after the District's fiscal year end (Sept 30), landing in late March/early April each year. The FY2025 report is the current one already posted (published April 2026), so the next expected edition (FYE 9/30/2026) would be released around late March-April 2027, following the observed pattern.

reports.title: Harris County Hospital District (Harris Health) audited financial statements
reports.description: Annual audited statements of the county hospital district, a component unit of Harris County whose board is appointed and whose tax rate is approved by Commissioners Court. Its own levy was $0.18761 per $100 for 2025 — roughly four times the flood control rate, for a service Californian counties fund out of realigned state revenue instead.

entries.covers: FY2024 (year ended Sept 30, 2024) audited financial statements - auditor's report date
FY2025 (year ended Sept 30, 2025) audited financial statements - auditor's report date
FY2026 (year ending Sept 30, 2026) audited financial statements - projected next release

release_schedule.note: Harris Health changed its fiscal year end from Feb 28/29 to Sept 30, effective with a stub year ended Sept 30, 2022 (previously FY ran March 1 - Feb 28/29). Since the change, audited combined financial statements (auditor's report by Forvis Mazars, LLP) have been issued in mid-February of the following calendar year: FY2024 statements dated Feb 13, 2025 and FY2025 statements dated Feb 11, 2026 (already published as of today, 2026-08-11). No published release calendar or statutory deadline was found stating an exact required date; this is inferred from the two most recent post-fiscal-year-change releases, which fell 4-4.5 months after fiscal year end. Next expected release: audited financial statements for FY2026 (year ending Sept 30, 2026), likely around February 2027.

reports.title: Port of Houston Authority Annual Comprehensive Financial Report
reports.description: The calendar-year financial report of the port authority. Structurally odd and worth having for exactly that reason: the Authority is a primary government and explicitly not a component unit of the county or of any city, yet Harris County Commissioners Court levies an ad valorem tax on its behalf and the county Assessor-Collector bills and collects it, with the proceeds funding general obligation debt service only.

reports.title: Toll Road Enterprise Fund of Harris County — basic financial statements
reports.description: The contrast case in the Texas district layer: the toll road authority is a department and enterprise fund of the county rather than an independent taxing unit, and drew 90.8 percent of its revenue from tolls in fiscal 2024. It levies no tax of its own, though legacy tax bonds remain secured by a pledge of the county's unlimited taxing power — so the contrast is "no own levy", not "no tax nexus".

entries.covers: FY2023 (year ended 9/30/2023) basic financial statements - auditor's report date
FY2024 (year ended 9/30/2024) basic financial statements - auditor's report date
FY2025 (year ended 9/30/2025) basic financial statements - auditor's report dated 4/7/2026, posted online 4/21/2026
FY2026 (year ended 9/30/2026) basic financial statements - projected next release based on observed pattern

release_schedule.note: Fiscal year ends 9/30. Confirmed via three consecutive editions: FY2023 statements dated 3/28/2024, FY2024 statements dated 3/28/2025, and FY2025 statements dated 4/7/2026 (Deloitte & Touche auditor's report) and posted on hctra.org on 4/21/2026 (per Houston Strategies blog, which links the actual FY2025 PDF at https://www.hctra.org/-/media/2ba0076447b44da0948e12147ce7a26b.ashx). No published release calendar or statutory day-certain deadline specific to this fund was found (Texas Local Gov Code 114.025, referenced in the FY2024 filing, sets an April commissioners-court filing deadline for the county auditor's general annual report, but that is a distinct, broader county filing, not a dated calendar for this specific enterprise-fund financial statement). Pattern indicates next release (FY2026, FYE 9/30/2026) is expected ~March-April 2027. The corpus's existing url points to the FY2024 edition, which is now superseded by the FY2025 edition released 4/21/2026 at a new dated-edition URL; no stable landing page listing all editions could be confirmed, so no url_correction is offered despite the current link being one edition out of date.

reports.title: Houston Community College System approved budget
reports.region: Harris County and Fort Bend County, Texas
reports.description: The annual budget of a junior college district, which in Texas is a taxing unit in its own right — the only post-secondary body anywhere in this corpus that levies a property tax. Ad valorem taxes were 52 percent of budgeted revenue in fiscal 2024, at $0.092231 per $100 on $281.6 billion of certified value drawn from two separate appraisal districts.

entries.covers: FY2028 Approved Operating Budget

release_schedule.note: No published budget calendar or statutory adoption date was found on HCC's site. Observed pattern: the Board of Trustees has approved the upcoming fiscal year's operating budget in late June in each of the last two documented cycles — FY2025 budget approved 2024-06-26 and FY2026 budget approved 2025-06-25 (fiscal year runs Sept 1–Aug 31). The FY2027 budget approval (expected around June 2026) could not be directly confirmed via search, so the projected next entry is for the FY2028 budget (~June 2027), based on the observed pattern.

reports.title: Harris County Emergency Services District annual financial report
reports.description: The audited annual report of an emergency services district — independent taxing units under Health and Safety Code chapter 775 that fund fire and ambulance service. Because Harris County exceeds three million people, §775.0825 requires the audit by July 1 and filing with the clerk of Commissioners Court within thirty days. Modelled on District No. 9 as the retrievable instance of a class.

entries.covers: FY2026 annual audit/financial report for each Harris County Emergency Services District

release_schedule.rule: A district shall prepare on or before July 1 of each year an audit of the district's fiscal accounts and records. (This section, Tex. Health & Safety Code § 775.0825, applies only to a district located wholly in a county with a population of more than three million — i.e., Harris County ESDs, as distinct from § 775.082's June 1 deadline for ESDs in less populous counties.) A copy of the audit must then be filed with the clerk of the county commissioners court within 30 days after the board receives it.
release_schedule.note: The July 1, 2026 deadline for this cycle has already passed as of the reference date (2026-08-11), so the next occurrence is July 1, 2027. Harris County has ~60+ separate Emergency Services Districts (ESD 1, ESD 9, ESD 11, ESD 14, ESD 15, ESD 17, ESD 46, ESD 75, ESD 80, etc.), each governed by this same statutory deadline and each publishing its own audit independently — there is no single unified 'Harris County ESD' report.

dependencies.basis: Government Code §30052(a) makes the allocation a pure share of measured retail activity: the accounts are "continuously appropriated, without regard to fiscal years, to the Controller for allocation to each qualified county in proportion to its share of the total taxable sales in all qualified counties during the most recent calendar year for which sales have been reported." A county's public safety money therefore rises and falls with how much is bought in it.

reference_period.stated_as: The most recent calendar year for which taxable sales have been reported; the ratio is refreshed annually and applied to monthly receipts.

dependencies.basis: Revenue and Taxation Code §97.70 defines each entity's vehicle license fee adjustment amount for 2005-06 and every year after as the prior year's amount multiplied by "the percentage change from the prior fiscal year to the current fiscal year in gross taxable assessed valuation" within that entity's jurisdiction, with the county auditor computing and certifying the figure for the county and each city under §97.70(c)(5). The gross taxable assessed valuation comes off the county assessor's roll — so a payment named for vehicles is in fact a function of property value.

reference_period.stated_as: The change in gross taxable assessed valuation between two fiscal years, each measured on the January 1 lien date; certification due June 30.

dependencies.basis: The Controller's county reporting instructions state that "Pursuant to Government Code section 12463 ... the data used for the financial transactions report come from audited financial statements, if available", and instruct counties that reported amounts should agree with what they report in their own annual comprehensive financial report for the year. The Controller's compilation is therefore downstream of every county's audited statements.

reference_period.stated_as: The county fiscal year just closed; filings due within seven months of year end.

dependencies.basis: The same instructions direct counties to the Controller's Accounting Standards and Procedures for Counties manual, which "conforms to Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) as prescribed by the Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB)", and prescribe modified accrual for governmental funds and full accrual for proprietary and fiduciary funds.

Government Code §30029.05 provides that Local Revenue Fund 2011 money "shall be allocated ... pursuant to schedules developed by the Department of Finance in consultation with the California State Association of Counties", and that the Controller "shall allocate these funds pursuant to the base allocation schedule provided by the Department of Finance for that fiscal year". §30029.07 applies the same mechanism to the growth account. The Governor's Budget item for 2011 State-Local Realignment is the Department's published statement of those amounts.

Welfare and Institutions Code §17606.20(b)(5) provides that general growth allocations from the Sales Tax Growth Account "shall be determined based on schedules developed by the Department of Finance" in consultation with the county associations. The Department's published statement is the Governor's Budget item for 1991 State-Local Realignment, which sets out the sales tax, vehicle license fee and growth accounts and records that they are continuously appropriated for allocation to local governments according to formula.

The Tax Office states that "When the certified appraisal roll is received from the Harris Central Appraisal District, the property values are loaded into the Tax Office's internally developed computer system", and that the office "maintains approximately 1.5 million tax accounts and collects property taxes for 70 taxing entities including Harris County." Tax Code §26.01(a) supplies the mechanism: "By July 25, the chief appraiser shall prepare and certify to the assessor for each taxing unit participating in the district that part of the appraisal roll for the district that lists the property taxable by the unit."

reference_period.stated_as: Values as of the January 1 appraisal date, certified by July 25; the 2025 worksheets were signed on 1 August 2025.

dependencies.basis: The published summary carries the caption "Truth in Taxation Summary Provided in accordance with Texas Property Tax Code, § 26.16", and the per-jurisdiction worksheets state that "Tax Code Section 26.04(c) requires an officer or employee designated by the governing body to calculate the no-new-revenue (NNR) tax rate and voter-approval tax rate for the taxing unit."

The District's own rate calculation worksheet states that "The calculation process starts after the chief appraiser delivers to the taxing unit the certified appraisal roll and the estimated values of properties under protest", with the total current year taxable value taken from that roll. The Harris County Tax Assessor-Collector signs it, certifying she "accurately calculated the tax rates using values that are the same as the values shown in the taxing unit's certified appraisal roll."

reference_period.stated_as: January 1 appraisal date; worksheet signed 1 August 2025 for the 2025 rate.

dependencies.basis: The District sets its rate through the same no-new-revenue and voter-approval framework as every other Texas taxing unit; the adoption notice carries the statutory comparison language, "THE TAX RATE WILL EFFECTIVELY BE RAISED BY 3.49 PERCENT".

The District's statements record that "On January 1, at the time of assessment, an enforceable lien is attached to the property for property taxes", and refer to subsequent adjustments to the tax rolls. Its rate calculation worksheet, filed under "Harris County Hospital District dba Harris Health", is built from the certified appraisal roll and signed by the county Assessor-Collector; Commissioners Court adopted a 2025 rate of $0.18761 per $100.

reference_period.stated_as: Lien attaches on January 1 at the time of assessment.

dependencies.basis: The statements record the division of labour plainly: "The Harris County Commissioners' Court approves the System's tax rate and annual operating and capital budget", and "The taxes are collected by the Harris County Tax Assessor-Collector and are remitted to the System as received." A hospital district that neither sets nor collects its own tax.

The hospital district's statements record that "The System is a component unit of Harris County, Texas (legally separate from Harris County, Texas), since the members of the System's governing board are appointed by the Harris County Commissioners' Court", so the district is consolidated into the county's reporting entity.

The Authority's report states that "Property is appraised, and a lien on such property becomes enforceable, as of January 1, subject to certain procedures", and that "Property taxes are generally levied in October or November for the year in which assessed." Its rate calculation worksheet, filed under "Port of Houston Authority", is computed from the certified appraisal roll and signed by the county Assessor-Collector.

reference_period.stated_as: Appraisal and lien as of January 1; levy in October or November.

dependencies.basis: The Authority states that "Debt service on Port Houston outstanding tax bonds is funded entirely from ad valorem taxes levied by the Harris County Commissioners Court on behalf of Port Houston", and that "Taxes are invoiced and collected by the Harris County Tax Assessor-Collector, which charges a fee for those services." It is nonetheless not a component unit — no county or city "exercises financial control over the Authority" — which makes it a body taxed for but not owned by the county.

The toll road statements record that "The Authority is a department and fund of the County and is included in the County's financial statements." Unlike the hospital district, this is not a component unit consolidated in — it is part of the county outright, and the distinction is exactly why one levies a tax and the other does not.

The college's budget builds ad valorem tax revenue — 52 percent of budgeted revenue, $205.7 million — on certified values from the Harris County and Fort Bend County appraisal districts: "Taxable values totaled $281.6B, which is a 10.2% increase compared to prior year certified values", at an adopted rate of $0.092231 per $100.

The college publishes a no-new-revenue rate and a voter-approval rate like any other taxing unit, noting that "The 86th Texas Legislature modified the manner in which the voter-approval tax rate is calculated to limit the rate of growth of property taxes in the state", and that the calculation uses July estimated values from the counties pending certification.

reference_period.stated_as: July estimated values, superseded by the certified roll.

dependencies.basis: District No. 9's audited report states that "All property values and exempt status, if any, are determined by the appraisal district", and the rate calculation worksheets for the county's emergency services districts are computed from the certified appraisal roll and signed by the county Assessor-Collector.

Health and Safety Code §775.074 provides that "The board shall annually impose an ad valorem tax on all real and personal property located in the district" and must certify that rate "to the county tax assessor-collector, who is the assessor-collector for the district". District No. 9 records paying the county Assessor-Collector $164,267 for assessment and collection services in one year.

_dropped.why: A negative finding worth as much as any edge here. The 1991 Realignment base reads nothing: Welfare and Institutions Code §17604 fixes 1991-92 base-year percentages of the vehicle license fee account county by county (Los Angeles 37.26 percent, San Francisco 7.15, Orange 5.43) and then directs the Controller to deposit "until the deposits equal the amounts that were allocated ... in the prior fiscal year". The growth allocation is no better — §17606.10 references "the percentage of total state resources received in the 1990-91 fiscal year" and a report dated September 1991. A transfer of several billion dollars a year runs on a ratchet against a thirty-five-year-old snapshot, and names no population estimate, price index or current series at all.

_dropped.edge: in-home supportive services county maintenance of effort -> a price index
_dropped.why: Checked specifically because California indexes so much else, and the answer is no. Welfare and Institutions Code §12306.16 provides that "Beginning on July 1, 2020, and annually thereafter, the rebased County IHSS MOE from the previous year shall be adjusted by an inflation factor of 4 percent" — a flat statutory number, not a measured one. The pre-2019 version conditioned a 5 or 7 percent factor on whether realignment revenues grew, which is a revenue test, still not a price index. So the county share of in-home care escalates at a rate the Legislature named once.

Only the county-level split reads a current series. Government Code §§30054-30055 allocate the within-county share to cities on their proportionate 1993-94 property tax loss from the second phase of the education revenue augmentation shift, reduced by a one-time 1993-94 transport account receipt, with everything unallocated going to the county — and cities that received no property tax or did not exist in 1980 are ineligible outright. So one half of this transfer is a live measurement and the other half is a photograph of 1993.

Checked and refused, because it is the obvious guess. The Necessities Index drives the CalWORKs grant level under Welfare and Institutions Code §11453, which is already an edge in the corpus, but no county allocation reads it. §17600.15 provides only that the child poverty subaccount deposits "equal the amounts that were deposited in the prior fiscal year", and §17600.50 allocates on 1991 historical amounts. The index sets what a family receives, not what a county receives.

The District publishes separate audited statements at a stable, predictably named path under the County Auditor's site, but that site's robots.txt disallows the entire directory the reports live in, so a compliant fetcher gets nothing. Its own site, hcfcd.org, publishes no financial documents at all. Every claim above is therefore evidenced from the tax rate worksheets and adoption notices instead. Publishes, but not readable.

The disclosure channel is split and only half of it is addressable. Rate documents are excellent — every district's worksheet sits at a predictable URL on the Assessor-Collector's site. Audited financials, required by §775.0825 to be filed with the clerk of Commissioners Court, surface only as agenda attachments with opaque identifiers and no per-district path. This is the emergency services district version of the problem already recorded for municipal utility districts, and it is the same shape: the tax is public, the accounts are not.

No college document names the Harris County Assessor-Collector as its collector, and the college's own posted rate worksheet now returns a 404. It also spans two appraisal districts, so the collection arrangement may not be uniform across its territory. Plausible and uncited.

_dropped.edge: harris county auditor as a node
_dropped.why: The Auditor prepares the county, flood control and toll road reports — the toll road statements are signed by the Auditor personally — but no retrievable document states the office's statutory duties or its mandate to prepare them. _dropped.why: The claim is almost certainly right and is the structural reason this whole district layer exists, but the section usually cited for it has been renumbered and now addresses abandoned lots. The evidence held is a county association handout listing counties' enumerated ordinance powers and a university research centre article stating that county land-use authority "does not include zoning but does include platting". Good enough for context, not good enough for a statutory citation.
